samples.text:
In democratic countries, important decisions are usually made by the government. However, some people think that the public should decide important national issues directly by voting in referendums, while others believe politicians and experts should make these decisions. I will discuss both side in this essay.

Some people support referendums because they are the most democratic way to decide. In a referendum, every citizen can vote, so the result shows what the majority of people really want. This can make people feel more involved in politics and trust the government more. Also, politicians sometimes do not keep their promises, so a referendum give ordinary people more power to control important decisions.

However, there are also problems with referendums. Many national issues are very complicated, for example economy or international agreements, and most people do not have enough knowledge to understand them. As a result, people may vote because of emotions or false information on social media. In contrast, experts have studied these topics for many years and politicians have advisers to help them, so they can make more better decisions. Moreover, organising a referendum is very expensive and take a long time.

In my opinion, most decisions should be made by elected politicians with the help of experts. This is why we vote for politicians, because we trust them to make difficult decisions for us. However, for some very important issues, such as changing the constitution, a referendum can be useful.

In conclusion, referendums are democratic but they have some risks. I believe that elected politicians and experts should make most national decisions, but people can vote directly for a few very important issues.

samples.text:
In most democracies, citizens elect representatives who then make decisions on their behalf. However, some people argue that major national issues should be decided directly by the public through referendums, while others maintain that such decisions are better left to politicians and experts. In my view, representative decision-making should remain the norm, with referendums used only in exceptional cases.

Supporters of referendums see them as the purest form of democracy. When citizens vote directly on an issue, the outcome clearly reflects the will of the majority, which gives the decision strong legitimacy. Referendums can also increase public engagement in politics, as people are encouraged to research and discuss the issues at stake. In addition, they offer a way to settle questions on which politicians are deeply divided or seem out of touch with voters.

On the other hand, there are significant drawbacks. Many national decisions, such as trade agreements or economic reforms, are highly complex and involve consequences that are difficult to predict. Most voters do not have the time or expertise to study these in detail, so campaigns are often dominated by simplified slogans or even misinformation. Furthermore, a referendum reduces a complicated issue to a simple yes-or-no choice, which leaves little room for compromise. Elected politicians, by contrast, can consult experts, negotiate and adjust policies over time, and they can be removed at the next election if the public are dissatisfied.

In my opinion, the advantages of representative democracy outweighs those of direct voting for most decisions. Referendums may be appropriate for fundamental constitutional questions, but even then the public should be given clear, balanced information before they vote.

In conclusion, although referendums give citizens a direct voice, I believe important national decisions are generally better made by elected politicians guided by expert advice, as they are better placed to deal with complexity and to be held accountable.
samples.why: Clear position throughout · both views extended and well supported · logical organisation with varied cohesive devices · good topic vocabulary (legitimacy, misinformation) · mostly accurate complex sentences with one agreement slip.

samples.text:
The question of how far ordinary citizens should be directly involved in national decision-making goes to the heart of what democracy means. Some believe that major issues should be settled by referendum, giving the public the final word, whereas others argue that such matters are better entrusted to elected representatives and specialists. While referendums have a place in a healthy democracy, I believe they are poorly suited to most important decisions.

The appeal of direct democracy is easy to understand. A referendum allows every voter to express a view on a specific question, producing a result that carries considerable moral authority. It can also re-engage citizens who feel alienated from mainstream politics, and it provides a means of resolving contentious issues that parliaments have been unable or unwilling to settle. From this perspective, entrusting decisions to politicians risks allowing a narrow political class to disregard public opinion.

However, the practical limitations of referendums are considerable. Many national questions involve intricate trade-offs, uncertain long-term consequences and technical detail that few voters have the time or background to evaluate thoroughly. In such circumstances, campaigns tend to reward emotive messaging over careful analysis, and misleading claims can prove decisive. Moreover, the binary format of a referendum forces a nuanced issue into a simple choice, leaving no scope for amendment or compromise, and the result can be extremely difficult to reverse. Representative institutions, by contrast, allow policies to be scrutinised, refined and revisited, while voters retain the power to remove politicians who fail them.

On balance, I believe that elected representatives, informed by expert advice, should make most important national decisions. Referendums can be justified for questions of fundamental constitutional significance, provided that voters have access to impartial information, but they should remain the exception rather than the rule.

In conclusion, although referendums offer a direct expression of the popular will, representative democracy is generally better equipped to handle complex decisions responsibly and accountably.
samples.why: Both views thoroughly developed and critically weighed · clear, qualified position · excellent logical progression · wide, precise vocabulary (binary format, alienated, scrutinised) · wide range of complex structures, error-free.
